outcome: Nothing has happened to this bullet since 26 January 2024 that I could find: no existence, nonexistence or bound result about (2,5)-perfect numbers appears in any source I opened. The only in-window items are a PrimePages curio that still poses σ(σ(n)) = 5n as open, and neighbouring work on iterates of σ and on quasiperfect numbers that does not address this equation.
problem_asks: Whether there exists at least one positive integer n with σ(σ(n)) = 5n, where σ is the sum-of-divisors function. The bullet names '(2,5)-perfect numbers' without defining them; the definition comes from the linked Wikipedia 'Superperfect number' article (Generalizations section) and the Cohen and te Riele notation: σ⁰(n) = n, σᵐ(n) = σ(σᵐ⁻¹(n)), and n is (m,k)-perfect when σᵐ(n) = kn, so (2,5) means σ(σ(n)) = 5n. Parts: (a) existence of one such n. The bullet asks nothing else: it does not ask for all such n, a count, finiteness, a classification, or the general (m,k) family. It has no parent bullet.

events.what_happened: G. L. Cohen and H. J. J. te Riele, 'Iterating the sum-of-divisors function', CWI report NM-R9525 (1995), later Experimental Mathematics 5(2), 1996, pp. 91–100 (Project Euclid; OEIS cites 93–100). Defines (m,k)-perfect numbers as σᵐ(n) = kn. Reports tabulating all (2,k)-perfect n below 10⁹, all (3,k)- and (4,k)-perfect n below 2·10⁸, and the least m for each n ≤ 1000. Poses open questions: for fixed m ≥ 1, are there infinitely many (m,k)-perfect numbers; is every n (m,k)-perfect for large enough m; limiting behaviour of σᵐ⁺¹(n)/σᵐ(n) and of (σᵐ(n))^(1/m). The table itself was not readable: the CWI and Project Euclid PDFs returned binary.
events.revisions: CWI report NM-R9525 (1995); journal version Experimental Mathematics 5(2) (1996), first on Project Euclid 13 March 2003 per the Project Euclid record. Month of the 1995 report not found.
events.delivers: A finite computer search for m = 2: all (2,k)-perfect n below 10⁹ (as stated in the abstract; the table was not read). It is a search bound for an existence question, so it moves no bound and settles nothing. If the table lists every k with a hit, it would show no (2,5)-perfect n below 10⁹; I could not confirm that from the table. The Wikipedia Superperfect table (m = 2 rows for k = 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14) has no k = 5 row, which I read as consistent with that, but it is an inference from an omission in a secondary list. The paper does not assert nonexistence for k = 5.
events.remains: Whether any (2,5)-perfect n exists at all: nothing above 10⁹ is covered by this search, and below 10⁹ the result is established only by inference from the secondary listings. The whole bullet remains open on this event alone.

events.what_happened: P. Cáceres and Z. Rafik, 'Iterating sum of power divisor function and New equivalence to the Riemann hypothesis', arXiv:2209.13010. The abstract I read says the paper investigates the dynamics of the iterated sum-of-divisors function σₖ(m) and its behaviour mod m, and notes that perfect and multiperfect numbers remain rare. Neither (m,k)-perfect numbers nor σ(σ(n)) = 5n appear in the abstract. A search summary also says the paper claims there is no m > 1 with σᵏ(m) ≡ 0 (mod m) for all k and an RH equivalence; I did not verify either claim. Neighbouring question, not this bullet.

events.what_happened: Z. Rafik and P. Cáceres, 'On Congruences for Iterates of the Sum–Power Divisor Function and Conditional Implications for the Riemann Hypothesis', arXiv:2102.09941 (2021; an html v2 exists). Takes up Cohen and te Riele's question whether for each n some iterate σᵏ(n) is divisible by n (they cite computations to 10⁹), and claims that no n > 1 satisfies σᵏ(n) ≡ 0 (mod n) for all k ≥ 1. Its text does not use the term '(m,k)-perfect'; it does not address σ(σ(n)) = 5n. Neighbouring question, not this bullet.

events.what_happened: A. Toyohara, Y. Tao and S. Yao, 'Every quasiperfect number has at least eight distinct prime factors', arXiv:2608.02066 (math.NT), submitted 3 August 2026. Claims that any quasiperfect number (σ(n) = 2n + 1, if one exists) has at least eight distinct prime factors, improving the seven of Hagis and Cohen (1982). Reports a finite computation with zero solutions, reproduced across independent ledgers, with lemmas formalised in Lean; and a coverage gap in a 2023 Zemann preprint with the same bound. This is a different problem (quasiperfect rather than (m,k)-perfect) and it does not mention σ(σ(n)) or 5-perfect numbers.

summary: No event bearing on (2,5)-perfect numbers was found in any opened source after 26 January 2024. The bullet's definition comes from the Wikipedia Superperfect number article (Generalizations): n is (m,k)-perfect when σᵐ(n) = kn, so (2,5) means σ(σ(n)) = 5n. The foundational source is Cohen and te Riele (CWI NM-R9525, 1995; Experimental Mathematics 5(2), 1996), which states a tabulation of all (2,k)-perfect n below 10⁹. Its PDF returned binary through my fetch tool, so I could not read the table. The Wikipedia table for m = 2 lists k = 2, 3, 4 and then 6 through 14, with no k = 5 row; the OEIS (2,k) entries I opened (A019287 for k = 10) give no (2,5) entry. I read the missing k = 5 row as consistent with no (2,5)-perfect n below 10⁹, but that is an inference from an omission in secondary listings, not a checked table, and an existence question is not settled by any finite search in any case. The clearest 'still open' evidence is PrimePages curio 46401, which poses σ(σ(n)) = 5n as an open question (submitted 2024-03-01, last modified 2025-02-27). Later arXiv work on iterates of σ (Rafik and Cáceres 2021; Cáceres and Rafik 2022, v2 December 2025) concerns divisibility of σᵏ(n) by n, not this equation, and does not treat k = 5. The only in-window paper with a model credited is arXiv:2608.02066 on quasiperfect numbers (σ(n) = 2n + 1), a different problem, whose acknowledgements name Anthropic's Claude per an automated summary. For the AI search I searched the problem name with AI terms, the Erdős-problem AI wiki, the OpenAI 2026 manuscript release, and the Anthropic and Google math announcements. None concerns (2,5) or perfect numbers. In the OpenAI openai/math release (719 manuscripts, 372 families), I read the family titles 001 to 377 and none concerns perfect numbers, divisor sums or iterated σ; manuscript bodies were not read. Close calls: (i) whether the k = 5 omission is a negative finding, which I record as an inference, not a result; (ii) whether a 2024 curio that poses the question is an event at all, which I record with delivers 'nothing'. Several search-summary claims were not opened and are not relied on: a Pomerance 'prime power' classification, an 'OpenAI odd perfect numbers' fragment that the OpenAI release does not corroborate, an EasyChair preprint claiming the infinitude of even perfect numbers is false, and a campusmoviefest blog about odd perfect numbers.
competing_reading: The Cohen and te Riele tabulation to 10⁹, with no (2,5) entry in the published listings, can be read as a substantive negative finding: the problem is 'no example below 10⁹', i.e. settled in the bounded sense, and the judging pass might count that as a restricted-case resolution. Against this, the bullet asks for existence over all n, so a finite search with no hit moves no bound on the question as stated and only shows that the smallest example, if one exists, is above 10⁹ or absent from the tables. The inference from the Wikipedia omission rests on the table's contents, which I could not read.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The Cohen–te Riele table of (2,k)-perfect numbers below 10⁹ (CWI NM-R9525 or Experimental Mathematics 5(2), pp. 91–100), read directly to confirm that no k = 5 entry exists. (2) An OEIS entry for σ(σ(n)) = 5n (none was found; the nearest is A246802, a different equation) with its search bound. (3) Any explicit n with σ(σ(n)) = 5n, which can be checked by computing σ(σ(n)) and comparing with 5n; or a proof that none exists. (4) The full text of arXiv 2209.13010 v2 and 2102.09941 v2 to confirm they contain no (m,k)-perfect content. (5) Only for the neighbouring record: the full acknowledgements sentence of arXiv 2608.02066.

judgement.why: The statement asks only whether any n with σ(σ(n)) = 5n exists. Nothing in the record settles or bounds that. The Cohen–te Riele 1995 tabulation is a finite search (instances), and it predates the snapshot. The 2024 PrimePages curio only restates the question (none). The Rafik/Cáceres papers concern divisibility of σ-iterates by n, which is a different question (variant); the 2025 v2 is not shown to add new mathematics, so that event stays dated 2022. The 2026 quasiperfect paper is about a different problem (variant). Its AI role, generated, applies to that paper alone; per the acknowledgements summary, AI discovered and proved the lemmas. It has no bearing on this problem.
judgement.doubts: The AI credit for arXiv 2608.02066 rests on an automated summary of the acknowledgements and a truncated quote. This does not matter here, because that event is a variant. The record never confirmed from the primary table that no (2,5) entry exists below 10⁹.
